double quotation mark Staff from Fox, CBS and NBC are here but not shooting, as journalists wait to see whether the judge will issue a ruling after hearing arguments today. stories.title: Ministers reject dog ownership licence scheme
stories.summary: A taskforce had suggested new legal requirements could help promote dog control and reduce attacks.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 24 September 2026

Pet owners will not have to pay a fee to own a dog, after the government ruled out introducing a licensing scheme.

In a report, published on Thursday, , external a panel of animal experts suggested the government should consider new legal requirements for dog owners.

The panel did not reach an agreement on which rules should be adopted but the taskforce said any new laws should aim to promote better dog control, reduce the risk of dog attacks and avoid placing an "undue burden" on owners.

A spokesperson for the environment department said: "This is a welcome report and ministers are considering the taskforce's recommendations, however we will not be introducing a new dog licensing scheme."

The Dog Control Coalition - which includes the RSPCA, Battersea Dogs & Cats Home and the Royal Kennel Club - said it supported the recommendations in the report and that it was "vital" for the government to take action "as a matter of urgency".

A spokesperson for the coalition said: "Dog bite incidents continue to have serious consequences for people and dogs, and the time that has passed since the publication of The Middlesex Report, in 2021, makes it imperative that we now see progress."

The report made 20 recommendations including calling for councils to provide a service to tackle low-level dog control issues, improved recording of dog bite wounds and legal requirements for dog walkers.

Dog attacks are still rising - even after the XL bully ban Published 30 April

What are the rules for having an XL bully dog? Published 24 March 2025

Dog licences explored to tackle ownership issues Published 7 May

The Responsible Dog Ownership Taskforce was established by the government in 2022, following a series of high-profile dog attacks.

The taskforce's report noted that since 2011 the dog population in the UK had grown by 35%, while hospital admissions relating to dog bites in England had risen by 77%.

It said pet ownership had spiked during the Covid pandemic at a time when it was harder to access support services.

"This led to less experienced owners struggling to access services and finding it harder to get help," the report said.

Until 1987, dog owners in England, Wales and Scotland had to pay an annual fee to get an ownership licence.

The scheme was scrapped on the grounds that the amount of money it raised was outweighed by the operating costs.

Dog owners in Northern Ireland still have to buy a licence of £12.50, or £5 if the owner receives an income-related benefit.

In France, owners of the most dangerous dogs have to get special permits which can involve passing a training course and putting the dog through a behavioural assessment.

Switzerland previously required potential dog owners to complete a knowledge test, followed by a practical, but this condition has been scrapped.

The report said that most members of the taskforce backed introducing legal requirements for dog owners but "further consideration would be needed regarding the form that this should take".

"Any legal requirement would need careful consideration of its objective and not appear as a tax on already responsible dog owners.

"Reintroducing a universal dog licence may amount to another database of responsible owners or an administrative exercise with little public safety benefit or opportunity to promote responsible dog ownership."

It said options could include focusing a scheme on high-risk dogs, introducing background checks on owners and requiring potential owners to pass a knowledge test.

The Dogs Trust and the RSPCA have commissioned research into the costs and benefits of different systems and their conclusions are due to be published later this year.

In a ministerial foreword to the report, environment minister Baroness Hayman of Ullock said: "In recent years, we have seen a concerning rise in dog attacks, alongside changes in patterns of dog ownership."

She said the taskforce's report was an "important and timely contribution", adding: "As ministers, we are carefully considering the recommendations alongside the wider programme of work already under way."

stories.title: Greek PM urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles permanently
stories.summary: Andy Burnham said in 2023 the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".

stories.body:
Published 24 September 2026

The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece.

Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would "send a powerful signal" but would require "courage".

The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal.

Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return.

The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country's claim to the Elgin Marbles.

"Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it," he wrote on Thursday , external .

"Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures."

His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles.

Mitsotakis said he was "surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures", adding: "I do not believe it does."

"Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we 'borrow' parts of our own monument," he wrote.

Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good.

This would be a "decisive step", Mitsotakis said, that would "reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship".

Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".

For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that "ultimately it's an issue for the British Museum", adding that "legally that's where that issue rests".

Many of the Elgin Marbles originate from the Parthenon in Athens

British ambassador Lord Elgin was granted permission by the Ottoman Empire, the governing authority in Athens at the time, to remove some of the marble statues in the early 19th Century.

They were created between 447BC and 432BC to decorate the Temple of Athena - what is now known as the Parthenon, in the Acropolis in Athens.

After an 1816 parliamentary select committee deemed Elgin's actions legal, the sculptures entered the British Museum collection by an act of Parliament.

The Greeks dispute their removal was lawful and the demands to return the statues have been vocal.

The Parthenon gallery in the Acropolis Museum in the Greek capital was deliberately designed with spaces left for the sculptures in the British Museum.

Back in 2023, George Osborne, then the museum chair, told the BBC he was looking for a "more co-operative arrangement" after "quite a bitter disagreement" with the Greeks for more than 200 years.

Mitsotakis's latest comments appear to suggest a ramping up of rhetoric around the thorny issue once again.

Last month, Greece's health minister told Breitbart News he would like to see US President Donald Trump pressure the British to return the Parthenon pieces.

The British Museum's position - and that of the UK government - is that the law prevents the permanent return of items held in its collection, though loan agreements are common.

Campaigners point out that the British Museum Act could be amended. However, the UK government has not signalled that this is a priority.

stories.title: Drinking at football matches - would fans welcome it?
stories.summary: Andy Burnham has long championed a repeal of the ban which prevents football supporters from drinking alcohol in the view of the pitch. But do fans even want it?
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The law permits supporters at stadiums from the Premier League to National League to drink alcohol outside the ground and in concourses, but not in their seats

Published 24 September 2026

When UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham embarked on his trip to the United Nations in New York, he might not have been expecting a question about football fans drinking alcohol in grounds.

Burnham firmly believes the law that prevents supporters from having a beer at their seat during a match is outdated.

It's a position the Everton supporter has long held, and when asked was happy to reaffirm.

"I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination," said Burnham, who feels football fans are singled out compared to those of other sports and events.

There is no suggestion this is about to become official government policy, and last year MPs rejected a Conservative amendment to the Football Governance Bill that would have forced ministers to launch a formal consultation on scrapping the rule.

That was, of course, before Burnham returned to Downing Street.

It is a complicated and divisive issue, about not just safety. But is it something that match-going supporters actually want?

What the law says

Drinking alcohol at football grounds in England and Wales has been strictly controlled since the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act was introduced in 1985.

It was brought in to counter escalating hooliganism through the 1970s and into the 1980s.

The ban impacts clubs in the Premier League down to the National League. While beer can be sold, it must be consumed in areas that do not have a view of the pitch.

Yet fans who support teams in the National League North and South and below can drink alcohol around the pitch.

The ban is more strict in Scotland, with a law in place since 1981 that alcohol is only available in hospitality areas and not for other fans.

It was initially imposed following a riot during the 1980 Scottish Cup final between Rangers and Celtic at Hampden.

However, attitudes have been changing in recent seasons.

It was lifted as part of a pilot scheme last year, with several Scottish clubs selling alcohol in clearly defined, monitored areas of the stadiums. It started with lower-level clubs, eventually being extended to the Premiership.

The Scotland national team joined the trial for the friendlies against Japan and Curacao earlier this year. It has been extended to games against Switzerland on 29 September and Slovenia next month.

The Women's Super League in England has just completed two seasons of successful trials and the rule preventing drinking in the stands has now been removed by the league's governing company, WSL Football.

The women's game is not governed by the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act, enabling the competition organiser to make the change.

Is there support for the move within English football's corridors of power?

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in August the competition had not "got a specific view" and "we'd need to give it some really careful thought".

The English Football League, however, issued a statement on Thursday that said it would be "receptive to discussions around reviewing the current legislation".

It added member clubs had already provided "a mandate to lobby for appropriate reform" which had "not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding".

Fans' views differ on drinking in stands

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Should alcohol be allowed in football stands?

The Football Supporters' Association has for some time backed changing the law.

Like the prime minister, it considers it to be unfair on football fans.

"I think it is outdated," FSA chairman Tom Greatrex told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme.

"If you go to watch football in Germany or in other places around the world, then it's perfectly acceptable.

"It is civilised and appropriate. There's no reason why that shouldn't be the case for football fans, as it is for fans of rugby league, watching Oasis, or anything else that happens often in the same stadiums in the same seats."

The FSA's position is that clubs should have the choice, in consultation with supporters, to sell alcohol.

Clubs might want to offer it in all stands, others in designated areas, while a few might choose not to do so at all.

Other sports offer designated alcohol-free sections, something that football clubs may wish to copy for some families and supporters who do not consume alcohol because of their religion.

The FSA acknowledges this, but believes having the option to make such decisions is important.

It believes relaxing the law would be more popular the further down the leagues you go, where alcohol sales could potentially provide a crucial additional income stream.

The UK Football Policing Unit rejected the suggestion, arguing alcohol plays "a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour" and that "other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour" that football does.

Yet for Greatrex, there is already proof police are not open to ideas through their previous opposition to safe standing.

Before it was introduced four years ago, Mark Roberts, who has been the national lead for football policing since 2014, told the BBC it would make it "easier to throw missiles, engage in hate chanting, racism, sneak alcohol in, take cocaine" .

"[The police] were telling everybody that we couldn't have standing at football again, that it would jeopardise safety, " Greatrex said.

"Actually, what we saw then was a controlled, managed pilot projects to get that re-established.

"There hasn't been the level of disorder that some of the police sources were saying there would be. I think the police should have more of an open mind and engage in this in a sensible and mature way."

Scottish football has slowly started to relax the ban of alcohol sales at matches but fans continue to protest for this to move at a faster pace.

For many match-going fans, however, the prospect of beer being thrown and potential anti-social behaviour outweighs the opportunity to watch a game with a pint.

Dave, a Chelsea fan from Twickenham, told Nicky Campbell on BBC Radio 5 Live, that he was "100% against it".

"Have a look at some of the footage you see on social media at Boxpark, for instance. A goal goes in and there is beer and lager thrown everywhere," he said.

"I don't want to go round stinking of other people's beer and there is a fashion among certain supporters to throw their beer everywhere.

"If people can't go without drink for a 45-minute period there is something the matter with them."

Adrian, from Leicester, claimed it would be the "worst idea you could come up with".

"There is enough trouble with other things in football, with the flares, drug taking and other things," he added. "You throw the alcohol in as well. Football is tribal whereas other sports they aren't."

But Ryan, a Wolves fan in Banbury, said "a solution that suits everybody" is to provide designated areas for drinking in stands.

What is it like in other sports and different countries?

Football is in the only sport in the UK which faces restrictions on the consumption of alcohol.

Some of these sports have issues with alcohol-related and anti-social behaviour, but none have the same reputation as football.

The restrictions differ around Europe.

There is a strict ban in the top two divisions of Spanish football, where only alcohol-free beer can be sold outside of hospitality areas. It can, however, be taken to seats.

In the German Bundesliga, there is no ban on drinking at your seat. So relaxed is the approach to alcohol at games that you will even find people selling bottles of beer from shopping trolleys outside grounds.

In the Italian Serie A it is similarly as relaxed, though to a limit of 5% ABV. Some games which are designated "high risk" have sales suspended in and around the stadium.

In France, the Evin Law was introduced in 1991 which is pretty much in line with Scotland, as far as football is concerned. Alcohol cannot be sold at any sports event, other than in VIP areas.

stories.title: Teenagers to be offered new vocational GCSE subjects in school
stories.summary: New GCSE subjects could include child development and building and construction as vocational courses are being introduced.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 23 September 2026

New vocational GCSEs will be introduced from 2029 for 14-year-olds alongside existing core academic subjects in England.

The new subjects could include building and construction, business management and finance, and child development.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said there was "no question" that academic learning was at "the core of any education system", but said there was "huge demand" for subjects with more practical elements too.

Education unions said the ideas were welcome, but a clear strategy was needed to make them happen. The Conservatives said the plans risked "throwing away" progress made in recent years.

Standards for the new qualifications will be set nationally by the regulator Ofqual to ensure grades are in line with other GCSEs, and will gradually replace other qualifications at this level such as BTec tech awards.

The vocational GCSEs will be designed to allow teenagers to progress at 16 to studying similar courses at college, including the new V-levels , which schools and colleges are teaching from autumn 2027, and T-levels .

The idea is to create a clear pathway for teenagers into different types of work through a ladder of qualifications.

But the Liberal Democrats warned the new vocational GCSEs should not become a "pipeline" directing disadvantaged pupils away from more academic subjects.

Powell told the BBC she was "not going to oversee a two-tier education system".

"I want working class, disadvantaged young people to have every opportunity to achieve highly academically," she said.

"And I also want every child to have the opportunity to take on more vocational and technical subjects."

Powell told BBC Breakfast schools would be able to specialise in subjects relevant to the jobs available in their local areas, adding that she wanted to improve the "esteem, respect and recognition" of the current qualifications.

Asked whether there would be dedicated funding to help schools cover the cost of the new qualifications, she said the government would "work with the sector to make sure this is absolutely deliverable", and that ministers would "make sure any funding needed is made available".

A new national target for employers to help create 200,000 work experience opportunities for under-16s is also being set by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as part of reforms to shake-up the education system to better prepare young people for the world of work.

VCSEs , external , a new style of vocational qualification unique to Wales, will be taught in schools and colleges from September 2027.

Learners in Wales can choose from 15 VCSE subjects including Animal Care​, Nature Restoration​ and Motor Vehicle Maintenance​.

Daisy is taking business studies at BTec Level 2 - this is the kind of subject that could be replaced by a new Vocational GCSE

Vocational subjects at 16 currently make up 7% of the entries for qualifications in England and it is up to each school how many subjects with hands-on learning they offer.

Wright Robinson College in Gorton, East Manchester, already offers 10 practical or vocational subjects for study in Year 10.

Daisy, in Year 11, is taking business studies as a BTec Level 2 which she said is giving her "practical experience" and building her confidence to progress to an A-level in the subject.

This is the kind of subject that may be replaced by one of the new vocational GCSEs.

Many of these existing tech awards have their standards set by the examining organisations, not the regulator. The standards for the new vocational GCSEs will be national.

Sarjo, also Year 11, already knows she wants to be a flight attendant so she is taking hospitality and catering as a BTec Level 2 alongside GCSEs.

She said she "learns faster" in the practical subject and most teenagers want to do something they enjoy alongside core academic subjects.

Martin Haworth, executive head teacher at Wright Robinson College, said any new qualifications had to "add value" to what was already on offer and labelling them as GCSEs might help with credibility.

He said schools would need to recruit specialist staff if the courses and exams were going to be "robust", and it would cost schools money to convert existing classrooms for practical learning.

Sarjo enjoys the practical elements of her hospitality and catering BTec

New analysis of school funding by the independent Institute for Fiscal Studies shows the budget per pupil is growing faster than expected, by 9% in real terms between 2025-26 and 2028-29.

This is partly because of various government top-ups to the budget and falling pupil numbers in some areas.

Economist Luke Sibieta said asking schools to offer more vocational routes would be a "big change" on top of the significant reforms to support for pupils with special educational needs and disabilities.

He said there was a "big question mark" over whether there were enough people to teach technical and vocational subjects, with further education colleges already struggling to recruit.

The Association of Colleges (AoC) suggested schools worked with them because they could offer "industry standard facilities" and qualified staff.

David Hughes, from the AoC, said this would help ensure learning was "authentically different to school and properly employment focused".

Daniel Kebede, from the National Education Union, said "sustained investment and resources" was needed to make a success of the new qualifications.

While Pepe Di'Iasio, of the Association of School and College Leaders, described the government's plans as "well-intentioned", but not making sure schools had the staffing and resources would not remove barriers to young people.

He welcomed the national push for work experience and said with placements "extremely difficult" to secure, more support was needed from employers.

The existing statutory career guidelines for secondary schools in England already require "meaningful" work experience for 14 to 16-year-olds.

Employers are now being asked to contact their local careers hub to offer placements.

Laura Trott MP, who is the Conservative Party's shadow education secretary, said she was concerned the changes risked losing the progress England had made in improving standards, and "ripping up the system" could mean "sabotaging young people's futures".

"Better schools will continue to protect rigorous subjects but disadvantaged children will be steered towards easier routes, lowering expectations for the very pupils who need high standards most," she said.

stories.title: Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats
stories.summary: Use our interactive tracker to explore the latest migration statistics for the UK
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

Published 27 November 2025

Updated 24 September 2026

UK net migration has dropped to the lowest level, outside of the Covid pandemic, since 2012.

How does that sit alongside other key migration measures, including asylum applications, small boat arrivals and visas granted?

Scroll down to find out more about the latest key figures, and get answers to key questions on a range of topics.

UK migration data at a glance

Net migration (change in population), January 2025 to December 2025

Immigration (people arriving), January 2025 to December 2025

Emigration (people leaving), January 2025 to December 2025

Asylum applications, July 2025 to June 2026

Returns and deportations from the UK, July 2025 to June 2026

Arrivals by small boat, 1 January 2026 to 23 September 2026

Small boat crossings and other illegal arrivals

Between 1 January and 23 September 2026, a total of 18,565 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 42% on the same period the previous year.

These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.

Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.

Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026.

Boats that arrived in the UK from 24 September 2025 to 23 September 2026 carried an average of 67 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.

Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier . At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).

When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.

People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026.

In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.

Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year.

There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.

The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.

Asylum applications and hotels

An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence.

The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026.

About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) or former military sites .

The government has pledged to stop the use of hotels by 2029.

More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland.

A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive

Type in a postcode or the name of a local council below to see how many asylum seekers are housed in the area

A total of 85,891 people applied for asylum in the UK from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 21% on the same period in the previous year.

Most people who arrive in the UK by small boat claim asylum, but they were only 40% of all asylum seekers from July 2025 to June 2026.

The rest include people who arrived by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and applied for asylum while holding, or just after holding, a valid visa.

It can take years for the government to decide whether someone should be granted asylum.

In June 2026, 40,168 people - across 32,401 asylum applications - were waiting for an initial decision. The number of people awaiting an initial decision was down by 56% on the previous year.

As of June 2026, a further 90,341 refused asylum applications were part of a second backlog, waiting the outcome of an appeal in the courts. This was up by 51% on the previous year.

Together, these initial decision and appeal cases form the government’s total asylum applications backlog, which it has pledged to clear .

Refugee status was granted in about 38% of asylum decisions made by the Home Office from July 2025 to June 2026.

About 39% of asylum appeal cases concluded between January 2026 to December 2026 resulted in a previous refusal decision being overturned.

Returns and deportations from the UK

The government requires people who are in the UK, but no longer have permission to live or work in the country, to leave.

This is called a return and can happen voluntarily or involuntarily.

People can lose the right to be in the UK for different reasons, such as a visa expiring, an asylum claim being refused, or by receiving a criminal conviction that results in deportation.

There were 40,605 returns from July 2025 to June 2026. This was up by 8% on the same period the previous year.

That number of returns is equivalent to about 6% of total emigration from the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

Of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026:

5,962 had been convicted of a criminal offence 12,568 had lodged an asylum claim at some point 3,310 had arrived in the UK by small boat

People from India made up 27% of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026.

The UK is trialing a scheme with France to return people who arrived in the country on a small boat.

For every person the UK sends back to France, the UK will accept an equal number of asylum seekers.

This is called the "one in, one out" deal. As of 30 June 2026, 1,087 people have been returned through this arrangement.

Returns can happen in different ways. "Enforced returns", which includes deportations, means the government arranges transport to return people to a different country. In some cases, people are escorted by officers.

All other returns are "voluntary". This means a person has agreed to leave and may receive government help with travel and other costs to help facilitate the return.

Some people classed as leaving the country voluntarily do so completely independently and without any government knowledge or involvement .

Independent returns made up 34% of the total from July 2025 to June 2026.

Visas for legal migration

Most people who come to the UK do so legally, after being granted a visa before they travel.

A visa gives someone permission to enter or stay in the UK for a specific purpose, such as work, study or joining family members.

There were 727,487 people who came to the UK via visas from July 2025 to June 2026, not including visitors or people transiting through the UK. This was down by 15% on the same period the previous year.

That does not mean all those people travelled to the UK, only that they were approved to do so.

The most common type of visa people came to the UK on was study, which made up 53% of all visa entries from July 2025 to June 2026.

People from China were the most common group to come to the UK on study visas, making up 23% of the total.

Together, people from China and India accounted for nearly half of all study visas. This has been the case for many years.

Migration to Europe

The EU and UK monitor the number of people crossing borders in the Mediterranean and English Channel by sea without permission.

There were 139,288 sea arrivals to the UK, Greece, Italy, Spain and Cyprus from August 2025 to July 2026.

Crossings to the UK accounted for about 22% of the combined total.

Sea arrivals into mainland Europe peaked in 2015, when the UN said more than a million people crossed the Mediterranean.

The top three countries with the most people claiming asylum from April 2025 to March 2026 were Spain with 133,795, Italy with 124,740 and France with 111,320.

The UK ranked at number five for asylum claims over the same period when compared with 26 other European countries with populations over one million.

When adjusted for population size, the UK ranks at number 10 for asylum applications per 100,000 people.

Net migration measures the overall change in a country’s population due to migration over a given period. It is everyone coming into the country (immigration) minus everyone who leaves (emigration).

The latest available data to compare the UK with other European nations is January 2024 to December 2024.

At that point, the countries with the biggest increase in their population were Spain with 626,000, Germany with 494,000 and the UK with 331,000, after taking into account the people who left the country, and those who arrived.

When adjusting for population size, the UK was in position 11 for increase in population due to migration, alongside 13 other European countries with comparable data per 100,000 residents.

Is the government meeting its pledges on illegal immigration and asylum? Published 26 February

Why do Channel migrants want to come to the UK? Published 9 July 2025

Find out more about people crossing the Channel in small boats Published 22 October 2025

Produced by: Rob England, Libby Rogers, Jess Carr, Aidan McNamee, John Walton, Becky Dale, Allison Shultes, Chris Kay, Steven Connor and Scott Jarvis.

Graphics by: Jez Frazer, Zoe Bartholomew and Joy Roxas

About the data

Figures from government and other official sources can be revised between publications. This page shows data as presented in the latest available release.

Immigration, emigration and net migration

*The net migration figure for the UK will not exactly equal immigration minus emigration because the Office for National Statistics (ONS) publishes it as a rounded number.

Immigration and emigration estimates , external from the ONS are updated twice a year.

Net migration figures use the internationally recognised definition of a long-term migrant: "A person who moves to a country other than that of their usual residence for at least a year."

Visas for legal migration

The total number of visa entries only includes visas that have been granted. It does not include visitor visas or transit visas, where the UK is not the final destination.

Visa figures record when permission was granted, not when or whether someone arrived in the UK.

If a person was granted more than one visa within the year shown, each visa is counted separately.

Work visas refer to new individuals granted permission, or extensions of existing permission. This includes categories such as seasonal work, health and care, domestic worker and youth mobility visas.

Study visas include all individuals sponsored by approved UK education providers, as well as those on short-term study visas.

Family visas allow someone to come to or remain in the UK to live with close family members already here. This includes joining a spouse, partner, child or parent, or coming to care for a relative.

The "Other" category includes visas outside work, study and family routes. This covers humanitarian schemes such as the Ukraine Sponsorship Scheme and the British National (Overseas) route. It also includes family permits for people from European Union or European Economic Area countries.

Asylum applications and accommodation

Home Office figures for asylum seekers in hotels are published under the category "contingency accommodation - hotel".

The number of people in all other forms of accommodation includes non-hotel contingency accommodation, as well as initial, dispersal and "other" accommodation.

To show how evenly accommodation is distributed, a scale compares each local authority's share of people in that type of accommodation with the UK-wide average for areas using the same accommodation type:

Less than half – more than 50% below the average share

Lower than – between 25% and 50% below the average share

About the same as – within 25% of the average share

Higher than – between 25% and 100% above the average share

More than double – more than 100% above the average share

Backlog figures for people waiting for an initial asylum decision include both main applicants and dependants.

Open appeals against refused asylum applications refer to individuals. Figures on appeals are published every three months by the Ministry of Justice, at a different time from other government asylum statistics. It also includes a small number of appeals against revocation of protection.

Small boat crossings and other irregular arrivals

Small boat crossing figures and the average number of people per boat are taken from the Home Office daily data , external .

Entering the UK without permission is an offence under immigration law , external , but asylum seekers are generally not prosecuted if they claim asylum on arrival. In some cases, people have been prosecuted alongside other offences, such as people smuggling or re-entering after deportation.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) collects figures on people who have died , external or gone missing while crossing from mainland Europe to the UK. These reports are based on information from French and UK officials (such as police or coastguard) and media sources. The IOM considers them an undercount because there are no official statistics.

The figures may include people who died in the Channel itself, as well as those who died while travelling to a crossing point.

Data on modern slavery includes final decisions only. Modern slavery covers human trafficking, slavery, servitude and forced labour.

Figures for other entries without permission combine all recorded irregular arrivals that were not by small boat. This includes inadequately documented air arrivals, recorded detections at UK ports, and other recorded detections within the UK.

Returns and deportations

People who are denied entry at the border and then leave the UK are not included in the returns figures on this page.

Returns involving the government are grouped into three categories. Enforced returns (which include deportations) are cases where the Home Office requires someone to leave and arranges their removal, usually because they have no legal right to remain or following a criminal conviction.

Assisted voluntary returns are when someone agrees to leave the UK and receives government support, such as help with travel documents, flights or reintegration assistance.

Controlled voluntary returns are when someone leaves the UK voluntarily without being forcibly removed, but their departure is formally recorded by the Home Office.

Independent returns are referred to by the government as "other verified returns," and refer to individuals who have left the UK without

People returned after a criminal conviction include non-British citizens convicted in the UK of any criminal offence, or convicted abroad of a serious criminal offence.

UK migration compared with other countries

Sea arrival figures are taken from the UNHCR European sea arrivals dashboard and combined with UK Home Office small boat data.

Asylum application, immigration and emigration figures for European countries are the latest available data from Eurostat for: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Romania, Norway, Switzerland and Croatia.

UK population figures are from ONS, National Records of Scotland and the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency 2024 mid-year estimates. European population figures are from Eurostat as of 1 January 2024.

To ensure comparability with the UK, European countries with populations under one million are excluded from per-capita comparisons of net migration and asylum applications.

For net migration comparisons, only countries that include asylum seekers or refugees in their immigration figures are included.

These are: Austria, Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Slovenia, Spain and Switzerland.

Portugal was also excluded as it did not have net migration data available for 2024, it will be re-included in future updates.

stories.title: No 'switch' to stop small boats, Lucy Powell tells BBC
stories.summary: Labour's deputy leader was speaking to BBC local radio ahead of the party's annual conference
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Lucy Powell spoke to presenters from BBC local radio

Published 24 September 2026

There is no "switch" to stop small boat crossings, and not every migrant boat can be intercepted, Labour's deputy leader has told the BBC.

Lucy Powell's comments came after two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days, at Folkestone and Samphire Hoe in Kent.

The Home Secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, calling the failure to intercept the two boats "not acceptable".

But the Conservatives say Labour has lost control of Britain's borders, and a "radically different" approach is needed.

A total of 781 people were recorded as arriving in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest in a single day for far this year.

In a round of interviews with BBC local radio ahead of Labour's annual conference, Powell told BBC Solent: "We are taking all steps we can to really bear down on and eradicate the small boat crossings altogether.

"This has been a mammoth task across a whole range of different policy areas over the last couple of years, which is now starting to bear fruit, in that small boat crossings are significantly down this year - in fact significantly lower than at any time in the last six years.

"Obviously as we close down some avenues and we close down routes criminal gangs look to find new ways to deliver their terrible business model."

The thousands of migrants crossing the Channel are usually brought to shore by Border Security Command or RNLI boats.

Before Monday, no small boat arrivals to the UK coast without an escort had been officially recorded since September 6, 2025.

Uncontrolled landings are so rare that last year's incident was the only other one recorded since the Home Office began keeping data in 2023.

On Wednesday British rescue boats were sent to collect a group of migrants who had spent more than 33 hours at sea

Powell told BBC Kent: "It's not easy, if we had a switch that we could switch tomorrow to stop all small boats, we would switch it".

Labour's deputy leader and Education Secretary told Radio 4's Today programme that "(You) can't stop everything all of the time.

"Of course, it's a concern. That's why the Home Secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable."

The Conservative Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said on X: "Labour has lost control of our borders.

"A radically different approach is needed.

"We need to leave the ECHR so anyone entering Britain illegally can be rapidly deported. No hotels. No benefits. No lengthy court process. No asylum claim. Just rapid removal. Then the crossings will soon stop."

The Liberal Democrat home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson MP, said closer cooperation with the EU was key to tacking small boat crossings.

"Until the government adopts Liberal Democrat proposals to tackle the root cause by entering the EU's landmark Migration and Asylum Pact, these the smugglers will continue to find a way through, lives will be put at risk and taxpayers' money will be wasted," he said.

That’s the question dogging Westminster and the City. “The chancellor has probably lost about half the headroom he inherited, leaving it between £10bn to £15bn. As long as the headroom is in double figures, he will probably be able to avoid topping it up, but the drop in headroom means any additional day-to-day spending, such as on defence or cost of living, will have to be paid for by higher taxes. “What’s more, if the recent rise in energy prices is sustained through the next few months, household energy bills could rise by another 25% in January, which would take them above the level that the previous government capped them at. That would only further increase the pressure to act on cost of living by temporarily subsiding energy bills. “The PM and chancellor will be feeling quite claustrophobic today as the walls close in around them. Borrowing costs keep climbing, while borrowing itself is outpacing the teeny rise in tax receipts.
